title: L-1 Visa's 'Manager' Loophole Faces Growing Calls for Congressional Reform
excerpt: Allegations of visa misuse by major IT firms and a bipartisan reform bill have reignited debate over the L-1 program, which offers a fast track to U.S. permanent residency without many of the safeguards applied to H-1B workers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The L-1A visa's vague 'manager' definition allows misuse by IT firms, bypassing H-1B requirements.
  • Tata Consultancy Services received over 6,500 L-1A approvals, with fewer than 600 reported managerial roles.
  • The bipartisan reform bill proposes wage floors and penalties up to $150,000 for L-1 violations.
  • L-1A holders can transition to EB-1C green cards, bypassing lengthy labor certification processes.
  • Reform could protect legitimate workers but may also hinder skilled professional transfers from India.

A renewed push to reform the L-1 intracompany transfer visa is gaining traction on Capitol Hill, driven by whistleblower allegations against India's largest IT services firm and a long-dormant bipartisan bill that has found fresh relevance in the current immigration climate.

The L-1 program, created by Congress to let multinational companies move executives, managers, and specialized-knowledge employees across borders, has operated for decades with fewer guardrails than its better-known counterpart, the H-1B. Unlike the H-1B, the L-1 has no annual numerical cap, no prevailing wage requirement, and no lottery. Its utility hinges on a single, ambiguous term: "manager."

The 'Manager' Problem

Under immigration law, the L-1A visa is reserved for employees in executive or managerial capacities. But the statute also recognizes "functional managers" — workers who manage a function rather than supervise people. That distinction, critics argue, has become an invitation to abuse.

Earlier this year, a Bloomberg investigation brought the issue into sharper focus. Former employees of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) alleged in federal lawsuits under the False Claims Act that the Mumbai-based company obtained more than 6,500 L-1A visa approvals between October 2019 and September 2023 — a figure larger than the next six recipient companies combined, according to data obtained by Bloomberg from USCIS.

> **"The EEOC itself found "credible documentary evidence" that TCS "frequently falsifies documents in support of L-1 visa applications," according to a 2019 letter cited in the lawsuits."**

The discrepancy was stark. TCS's 2022 filing with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) listed fewer than 600 executive or managerial positions among its 31,000-strong U.S. workforce. The EEOC itself found "credible documentary evidence" that TCS "frequently falsifies documents in support of L-1 visa applications," according to a 2019 letter cited in the lawsuits. TCS has denied wrongdoing, stating it "rigorously adheres to all US laws."

A Fast Lane to Permanent Residency

What makes the L-1A designation especially consequential extends beyond temporary work authorization. Holders of the L-1A can apply for EB-1C green cards — a category for multinational managers and executives that bypasses the PERM labor certification process required of most employment-based applicants. That exemption eliminates months of recruitment testing and Department of Labor review, making the L-1A a direct gateway to permanent residency and, ultimately, U.S. citizenship.

"When companies seek to assign managerial titles to employees for the sole purpose of end-running other visa programs, the consequences should be real and painful."

— Daily Caller op-ed on L-1 reform, July 2026

For Indian nationals, who face EB-2 and EB-3 green card backlogs stretching beyond a decade, the EB-1C route through an L-1A is one of the fastest available paths. Current data shows L-1 transfers carry an approval rate of roughly 92%, according to immigration analytics firm Alma.

Bipartisan Reform on the Table

The H-1B and L-1 Visa Reform Act (S.2928), introduced by Senators Chuck Grassley (R-IA) and Dick Durbin (D-IL) in September 2025, directly targets several of these vulnerabilities. The bill, cosponsored by Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Bernie Sanders (I-VT), and Tommy Tuberville (R-AL), would impose mandatory wage floors on L-1 workers after their first year in the United States, aligning pay with Level II prevailing wages used in the H-1B program.

It would also restrict third-party placements — a practice common among IT consulting firms — requiring a Department of Labor waiver and proof that no U.S. workers were displaced. Penalties for violations would rise to as high as $150,000 per offense, with debarment from future visa participation for repeat offenders.

The bill has been referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and has not yet advanced to a vote.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

The debate over L-1 reform cuts both ways for Indian professionals in the United States. On one hand, tightening the definition of "manager" and adding wage protections could shield legitimate transferees from being undercut by companies gaming the system. Workers stuck in green card backlogs — many of them Indian nationals — stand to benefit if the EB-1C pathway is reserved for genuinely senior roles rather than repackaged mid-level positions.

"The EEOC itself found "credible documentary evidence" that TCS "frequently falsifies documents in support of L-1 visa applications," according to a 2019 letter cited in the lawsuits."

On the other, an overly broad crackdown risks collateral damage. Indian IT services firms remain among the largest users of the L-1 program, and any restriction that makes intracompany transfers more costly or difficult could slow the flow of skilled professionals between India and the United States.

The reform push arrives alongside a broader tightening of U.S. immigration policy. The Department of Homeland Security recently announced a new final rule capping student (F) and exchange visitor (J) visas at four years and limiting journalist (I) visas to 240 days. The U.S. Department of Labor has also launched a nationwide investigation into H-1B and PERM fraud.

Proposed Reforms to L-1 Visa
›Mandatory wage floors for L-1 workers after one year.
›Penalties up to $150,000 for L-1 violations.
›Restrictions on third-party placements.
›Bipartisan support from key senators.
Senate Judiciary Committee statement

What Comes Next

Congress faces a familiar tension: modernizing a program created before the era of remote work and global digital collaboration without undermining the legal immigration system that American businesses and skilled foreign workers both depend on. The question is whether lawmakers can write a definition of "manager" clear enough to close the loophole — and enforce it vigorously enough to make companies think twice before testing it.
